newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's plans wider check on market professionals.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's plans wider check on market professionals.

text.p: Lloyd's of London is considering whether to broaden a check on its working members next year to include insurance brokers, a move which could require thousands more professionals to be registered and submit to increased monitoring, said Lloyd's regulatory director David Gittings.

"We have in mind a plan to issue a broker consultation document with the Lloyd's 1997 regulatory document asking ways in which we've gone about regulating brokers and how that should change, bringing the framework more into line with the agency community," said Gittings in a recent interview.

Lloyd's this year introduced requirements that 3,000 directors and senior managers of underwriting agencies be registered. These agencies manage insurance syndicates, whose underwriters take on a slice of the risk in a Lloyd's policy.

The underwriters were the main targets for legal action by unhappy investors, who faced huge demands for cash after heavy losses at Lloyd's from 1988 to 1992 -- the result of a series of natural and man-made disasters and poor underwriting.
Together with auditors, brokers and members' agents, they contributed over 500 million pounds ($820 million) to a 3.2 billion settlement to compensate the investors, called Names, and end litigation.

Gittings said he regarded the period following completion in September of a recovery plan to reinsure the losses into a new company called Equitas as the last chance for the insurance market to weed out any unsuitable professionals still remaining and viewed registration of brokers as a logical step.

The consultation document containing proposals for applying to brokers regulatory measures imposed on agents would come out at the turn of the year and could address monitoring procedures and core principles in addition to registration.
Anthony Howland-Jackson, chairman of the Lloyd's Insurance Brokers' Committee (LIBC) which represents brokers' interests at the market, described registration as a "positive" move.

But he conceded there could be complaints about the cost and necessity of the process. There are about 220 brokers operating in Lloyd's and registration would require the co-operation of thousands in senior management, many of whom are already registered with the Insurance Broking Registration Council.
Lloyd's has processed half of the registration applications from the agency community. Of those left, it has unearthed 150 cases which need to be looked at more carefully, Gittings said.
Around twenty so far have either had strict conditions attached or been refused, including one who, like disgraced former Barings trader Nick Leeson, failed to disclose a court judgement against him.
Gittings estimated that five percent of all applicants could be unsuitable. Some may be named in court cases or loss reviews, others may fail credit reference or character suitability tests.

Lloyd's could in the future extend the registration requirements even further to include more junior ranking underwriters as well. But constraints on resources mean this is unlikely to happen at the same time as brokers are registered.
